consumer_pulse:
Discussion across r/PersonalFinanceCanada centred on the federal minimum-wage increase and whether it would translate into broader wage adjustments, with threads referencing the 6.7% unemployment rate and the government's EI extensions for tariff-affected workers. Users debated the practical impact on household budgets given that CPI sits at +1.8% year-over-year, with some noting grocery and shelter costs felt higher than headline inflation.

Cross-border travel remained a hot topic on r/CanadaTravel and related subreddits following the 22.0% plunge in Canadian return trips from the US. Posters attributed the decline to both tariff-related animosity and the weaker Canadian dollar implied by exchange-rate shifts. Google Trends data showed sustained elevated search interest in "Canada tariffs" and "EI extension" throughout March.

Housing affordability threads persisted on r/canadahousing, with users pointing to the $23.4 billion in January building-construction investment (down 1.9%) as evidence that supply remains constrained despite 250,900 annualized housing starts.

Capital project activity in Ontario during this reporting window was dominated by the Toronto transit funding announcement rather than resource-sector regulatory proceedings.

The policy rate at 2.25% reflects seven cumulative cuts from the Bank of Canada's peak rate of 5.00% reached in mid-2023, reducing carrying costs for Ontario's construction and development sector.
